claim: CLIP is trained on approximately 400 million image-text pairs collected from publicly available internet sources as the WebImageText (WIT) dataset.
notes: The paper describes 400 million image-text pairs; these are naturally noisy web pairs, not uniformly curated human labels.

claim: For a batch of N paired images and texts, CLIP compares all N×N possible pairings and maximizes the cosine similarity of the N true pairs while minimizing the N²−N mismatched pairings.
notes: The objective uses a symmetric cross-entropy over image-to-text and text-to-image similarity scores.

claim: The CLIP text encoder is a 12-layer, 512-wide Transformer with 8 attention heads and a 49,152-token BPE vocabulary; the maximum sequence length is 76 and the final EOS representation is projected.
notes: These are the paper's base text encoder details; do not assume every later CLIP-derived model keeps them.

claim: The paper trains five ResNet and three Vision Transformer variants for 32 epochs using Adam with decoupled weight decay and cosine learning-rate decay; the batch size is 32,768.
notes: The paper also describes mixed precision and memory-saving techniques. The largest ViT model uses 256 V100 GPUs for 12 days.

claim: The learnable temperature parameter is initialized to an equivalent of 0.07 and logit scaling is clipped to no more than 100 to avoid training instability.
notes: The implementation stores a log-parameterized multiplicative scalar; tau is not simply a permanently fixed hyperparameter.

claim: For zero-shot transfer, class names or descriptions are encoded by the text encoder, compared with image embeddings by cosine similarity, scaled by temperature, and normalized with softmax.
notes: The paper interprets the text encoder as generating weights for a linear classifier over image features.

claim: The paper reports 76.2% ImageNet accuracy and 95% top-5 accuracy for its best CLIP model in the zero-shot comparison.
locator: Table 1 and §3.1.3, Initial Comparison to Visual N-Grams
notes: The paper cautions that Visual N-Grams and CLIP differ in dataset scale, architecture, and compute; this is not a controlled comparison isolating the objective.

claim: Using the prompt template 'A photo of a {label}.' improves ImageNet accuracy by 1.3 percentage points over using only the label name; an 80-prompt ensemble improves the single-default-prompt result by a further 3.5 points on ImageNet.
notes: These are results under the paper's ImageNet evaluation setup, not a universal gain for every dataset.

claim: Zero-shot CLIP outperforms a supervised logistic-regression classifier trained on ResNet-50 features on 16 of the 27 datasets in the paper's Figure 5 comparison.
locator: Figure 5 and §3.1.5, Analysis of Zero-Shot CLIP Performance
notes: The paper also reports substantial variation by task; performance is not uniformly strong.

claim: CLIP has limitations on counting, distance estimation, fine-grained recognition, prompt sensitivity, out-of-distribution inputs, and social bias.
locator: Limitations and Broader impacts sections; cross-checked with the official model card
notes: The article does not present CLIP as a universal vision understanding system or a high-stakes classifier.

claim: The toy matrix values, temperature slider similarities, and pure-Python examples in this article are pedagogical constructions, not reported model outputs or a reproduction of the original training run.
locator: Independent teaching example based on §2.3 and §3.1.2
notes: The accompanying tests validate mathematical invariants only; they do not benchmark a trained CLIP model.

claim: The official CLIP model card positions the model as a research output, notes that it was not purposefully trained or evaluated for languages other than English, and flags unconstrained deployment, surveillance, and facial recognition as out of scope.
locator: Model Card: Model Use, Intended Use, Out-of-Scope Use Cases, Limitations
notes: The article presents these as the model card's stated scope and cautions, not as a new benchmark result.
